new_statements.quote: [verbatim fragments, joined with …] hebräische Wörter sind von Haus aus auf der vorletzten Silbe betont. In diesen Fällen ist die Betonung natürlich die gleiche geblieben, so z.B. kaudesch … Im übrigen war die Tonverschiebung zur vorletzten Silbe so häufig, daß sie vielen als die offizielle aschkenasische Betonung galt und … die aschkenasische Betonung der vorletzten Silbe häufig beibehalten wurde, wie z.B. in oneg schabbat. … ein Akzent über dem betreffenden Vokal [=] eine betonte lange Silbe; ein Punkt eine betonte kurze Silbe. Die Betonung isolierter Vokabeln (z.B. kaddisch, tachanun) steht normalerweise fest … a) berochaus: Zurückziehen der Betonung von der letzten auf die vorletzte Silbe
new_statements.translation: [Some] Hebrew words are stressed on the penultimate syllable to begin with. In those cases the stress has of course stayed the same, e.g. kaudesch … Otherwise the shift of stress to the penultimate syllable was so frequent that many took it to be the official Ashkenazic stress, and … the Ashkenazic stress on the penultimate syllable was often retained, e.g. in oneg schabbat. … an accent over the vowel in question [marks] a stressed long syllable; a dot a stressed short syllable. The stress of isolated words (e.g. kaddisch, tachanun) is normally fixed … a) berochaus: retraction of the stress from the last to the penultimate syllable

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stratum-dependent word stress, as in Yiddish generally: Hebrew/Aramaic-component words (the whole of Weinberg's religious vocabulary) carry the Ashkenazic penultimate stress, retracted from the Hebrew final syllable (berochaus < berakhót, kaudesch, schabbes), and the lexicon marks that stress on every headword because it is fixed for words in isolation; Germanic-component words keep the German root-initial pattern (not stated in the retrieved fragments; explicit for Yiddish as a whole in Katz 1993: 49, 'the Germanic component has root-bound stress.. Semitic component items, by contrast, exhibit penultimate stress'). Because placement depends on the lexical stratum (and on the Hebrew word's own shape), the reading is lexical/stratum-conditioned rather than a single positional rule, matching the catalog's 'lexical' code for Eastern Yiddish (east2295).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the retrieved fragments; Katz 1993 notes that a Germanic stem losing primary stress to a stressed suffix (lébadikərhéjt) retains stress and full vowel colour.
new_statements.exceptions: Weinberg: Hebrew words already penult-stressed in Hebrew keep that stress; in later usage Sephardic-influenced forms sometimes retain Ashkenazic penult stress (oneg schabbat); for certain entries (e.g. aumerbart) 'die Betonung liegt in diesen Fällen also nicht auf der vorletzten Silbe'; the editor occasionally 'corrected' a stress toward the grammatically 'right' side. Schäfer 2017: 245-247 shows WY ge-participles on non-initially-stressed (loan) verbs, implying non-initial stress in such Germanic-stratum loans.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: Weinberg explicitly speaks of 'Betonung isolierter Vokabeln' and marks stress on dictionary headwords; his material is the residual Jüdischdeutsch religious vocabulary of German Jews (north-German Ashkenazic pronunciation), not full sentences of a spoken WY dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Weinberg 1994 (and 1969) describe the 'Jüdischdeutsch' of German Jews before 1938: the residual Hebrew-component (religious) vocabulary of Western Yiddish embedded in German, in a north-German Ashkenazic pronunciation ('norddeutsch-aschkenasische Aussprache' per his own fragment), not a fully spoken WY dialect; Glottolog subsumes this under west2361 (no separate glottocode). Katz 1993's stress statement is pan-Yiddish with Northeastern Yiddish examples (east2295). Selig 1767 is 18th-century Saxon/Leipzig Jüdischdeutsch. Sources not opened cover Alsatian (Zuckerman 1969), Swiss Surbtal (Guggenheim-Grünberg 1958, Fleischer 2005) and Franconian (Klepsch 2004) WY.

sources.note: Sect. 9.6.2 'ge-Präfix bei sekundärem Wortakzent', pp. 245-247: in the modern standard systems of Yiddish and German only initially-stressed verb stems take the ge- participle prefix (citing Jacobs 2005: 213); particle verbs carry their own word stress; Western Yiddish sources attest ge- despite secondary word stress (wj. 'iz ward uffem danz gemarschirt', Die Hochzeit zu Grobsdorf 1822: 53). No general statement of where WY word stress falls; index 'Wortakzent 189, 245-247'.

sources.citation: Katz, Dovid. 1993. The phonology of Ashkenazic. In Lewis Glinert (ed.), Hebrew in Ashkenaz: A Language in Exile, 46-87. Oxford: OUP.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Printed p. 49 (the scanned text), framed as pan-Yiddish (Western and Eastern): 'the Germanic component has root-bound stress.. Semitic component items, by contrast, exhibit penultimate stress. Suffixation results in shift of stress to the newly penultimate syllable' (examples Northeastern Yiddish lébn, lébadik; málbas, malbúsim). Also pp. 48-49 divide Western Yiddish into NWY/MWY/SWY and give NWY stressed-vowel table (p. 53) but no WY-specific stress placement statement.
